what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Inertia, not AI, will decide the SaaS apocalypse
sections.para: Most medium and large SaaS companies will struggle spectacularly in the medium term as people build what they actually want. AI is available to both sides, so inertia decides: as with Nokia, which moved with nothing to protect and failed with fifteen years of success. Newcomers with nothing to protect are the ones to watch.

sections.label: The market already had this argument once this year
sections.line: The crash and recovery both priced in the database
sections.para: After Anthropic's Claude Cowork plug-ins in February 2026, the SaaSpocalypse wiped roughly $285 billion in about 48 hours before software recovered. The recovery argued the database is the moat, which concedes the interface is not. Both sides wrongly treated AI as the variable; Mark Murphy rightly said companies will not maintain bespoke replacements.

sections.label: First, the part nobody likes to say: users were never happy
sections.line: Users were frustrated, features unused, licences idle
sections.para: Freshworks found 91% of employees frustrated by workplace technology. Pendo found 80% of features rarely or never used, costing up to $29.5 billion, and Zylo puts unused licence waste at $21 million a year per organisation. Excel's persistence, with 73% preparing VAT returns in it, is the clearest evidence SaaS failed users.

sections.label: Why it got this way, in one line from Wardley
sections.line: Past success breeds inertia, and inertia breeds lock-in
sections.para: Wardley's climatic pattern explains it: an installed base resists change, and new entrants usually lead it. Large SaaS firms optimise for lock-in, so they neglect exports, schemas and first-class APIs. The map's claim is that SaaS has slid right towards commodity substrate, a database, bus or state machine, on which higher-order things get built.

sections.label: Everybody was already vibe coding, just very slowly
sections.line: Product owners always vibe coded, with a slow loop
sections.para: Karpathy's term from February 2025 became Collins' word of the year, and it describes writing very good briefs. Product owners always did that, but execution took weeks or months. Now the loop is minutes, so users can build the 10% they need, without the bloat.

sections.label: And the reason the incumbents cannot simply do this themselves
sections.line: SaaS companies are highly inefficient at developing software
sections.para: Large software firms neglected non-functional requirements like security, documentation, CI and refactoring under slogans like do not gold-plate. Stripe found developers spend 42% of their time on maintenance and bad code, and DORA 2024 found only 19% of teams elite. The constraint is the missing explorer, villager, town-planner handover, not money or models.

sections.label: The irony, which is the whole article in one paragraph
sections.line: What SaaS refused to build is what agents need
sections.para: Portability, open schemas, a real API at the centre, exportable data and callable capabilities were starved for twenty years as churn risks. The customer's agent now wants exactly that list and finds products built to prevent it. The moat now blocks the water in both directions.

sections.label: The mistake, and where the money actually is
sections.line: A brief is not a product; maintenance pays
sections.para: People bought SaaS because it is maintained, secured and versioned, and vibe coders will not maintain what they build, as Murphy argued. The future is village and town-planner companies running finished briefs, paid by consumption, plus some incumbents turned platforms and an explosion of solid components, since vibe-coded software is not automatically good.

sections.label: Strip the UI and see what is left
sections.line: Strip the UI and SaaS is a glorified database
sections.para: Without the interface, most of these companies are a glorified database, messaging system and state machine. That can be built, but it is very hard to build well, so the value has moved down a layer to the substrate and across to whoever runs and maintains it.

sections.label: More engineers, not fewer
sections.line: More engineers will be needed, and inertia decides survival
sections.para: Far more code will need reading, hardening and running, so we need as many developers or more, focused on excellence. Agents may beat Brooks's law by scaling communication in larger teams. Failure comes by default to firms protecting the screen and locked data; newcomers, with nothing to protect, have already moved.
